draft.title: The Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme
card: The Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme (PBS) is an Australian Government program. It subsidises many prescription medicines, which means the government pays part of the cost.
Because of the subsidy, a PBS medicine costs a patient less than its full price. The patient pays a set amount towards each script, and there is a maximum a general patient pays.
Concession card holders pay a lower amount again. Concession cards are for groups such as pensioners and some people on low incomes.
Only medicines listed on the PBS are subsidised, and a doctor must prescribe them. Many other medicines are not listed, so the patient pays the full price.
draft.remember: The PBS lowers the cost of listed prescription medicines, and lowers it more for concession card holders.

a.q: What does the PBS do for a patient who is prescribed a listed medicine?
opts: The government pays part of the cost, so they pay less
The patient pays nothing, because the medicine is free
The patient pays the full price and claims it back later
The government chooses which doctor the patient must see
a.why: The PBS is a subsidy, so the government pays part of the price and the patient pays a set amount. It does not make medicines free for everyone, because patients still pay something towards each script.
a.clue: A subsidy means the government pays only part.

b.q: Two people are prescribed the same PBS-listed medicine at a pharmacy in Bendigo. Sam holds a concession card and Jo does not. Which statement is correct?
opts: Both pay less than full price, and Sam pays less than Jo
Both pay the same, because the medicine is the same
Only Sam gets a subsidy, because Jo has no card
Jo pays less than Sam, because Jo pays the full price
b.why: The subsidy applies to everyone for a listed medicine, so both pay less than the full price. Concession card holders pay a lower amount again, so Sam pays less than Jo. The tempting wrong answer says only card holders get a subsidy, but the card gives an extra reduction.
b.clue: Everyone gets the subsidy, and the card adds more.

a.best: The government pays part of the cost, so they pay less

b.best: Both pay less than full price, and Sam pays less than Jo

problems.detail: 'A doctor must prescribe them' is not quite right: nurse practitioners, authorised midwives, dentists and optometrists can also write PBS prescriptions for some medicines. Better: 'a doctor or other authorised prescriber'.

'A PBS medicine costs a patient less than its full price' is not always true. When a listed medicine's price is below the general co-payment, a general patient pays the full (lower) price and gets no subsidy. A 'can' or 'usually' is needed.

The right option says both pay less than full price. For a low-cost PBS medicine priced under the general co-payment, Jo would pay the full price, so this is not true in every case. It holds for most medicines, but the card and the why state it as universal.
The clue 'Everyone gets the subsidy, and the card adds more' all but restates the right option, so a student can pick it without knowing the idea.
The clue 'A subsidy means the government pays only part' matches the wording of the right option ('pays part of the cost'), so it gives the answer away.

check.summary: Both questions have one clear right answer, but the card overstates two things: only doctors can prescribe PBS medicines, and every PBS medicine costs less than full price (not true for medicines priced below the co-payment). The clues also give the answers away, especially in question b.

proposal.title: The Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme
card: The Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme (PBS) is an Australian Government program. It subsidises many prescription medicines, which means the government pays part of the cost.

For most listed medicines, the patient pays a set amount per script, called a co-payment, and the government pays the rest. If a medicine costs less than the co-payment, the patient just pays its price.
Concession card holders pay a lower co-payment again. Concession cards are for groups such as pensioners and some people on low incomes.
Only listed medicines are subsidised, and a doctor or other authorised prescriber must prescribe them. For medicines not listed, the patient usually pays the full price.
proposal.remember: The PBS usually cuts the cost of listed medicines, and cuts it further for concession card holders.

a.q: What does the PBS do for a patient prescribed an expensive listed medicine?
opts: The government covers part of the price, so they pay less
The medicine is free, so the patient pays nothing at all
The patient pays full price, then claims it all back later
The government picks which pharmacy the patient must use
a.why: For an expensive listed medicine, the patient pays a co-payment and the government pays the rest, so the patient pays less than the full price. It is not free, because the patient still pays the co-payment at the pharmacy.
a.clue: Think about what happens at the pharmacy counter.

b.q: Sam and Jo are each prescribed the same expensive PBS-listed medicine at a pharmacy in Bendigo. Sam holds a concession card and Jo does not. Which statement is correct?
opts: Both pay less than full price, and Sam pays less than Jo
Both pay the same, because the medicine is the same
Only Sam pays less than full price, as Jo has no card
Jo pays less than Sam, as general patients get more help
b.why: For an expensive listed medicine, the government pays part for every patient, so Jo pays the general co-payment and Sam pays the lower concession co-payment. The tempting wrong answer says only card holders are helped, but the concession card only adds a further reduction.
b.clue: Work out what a general patient pays first, then the card holder.

a.best: The government covers part of the price, so they pay less

b.best: Both pay less than full price, and Sam pays less than Jo
